title: Soviet-Era Illustrations of J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit (1976)
description:
in Art, Literature |   	October 14th, 2026  Leave a Comment

body:
in Art, Literature |   	October 14th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Until I read J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings, my favorite book grow­ing up was, by far, The Hob­bit. Grow­ing up in Rus­sia, how­ev­er, meant that instead of Tolkien’s Eng­lish ver­sion, my par­ents read me a Russ­ian trans­la­tion. To me, the trans­la­tion eas­i­ly matched the pace and won­der of Tolkien’s orig­i­nal. Look­ing back, The Hob­bit prob­a­bly made such an indeli­ble impres­sion on me because Tolkien’s tale was alto­geth­er dif­fer­ent than the Russ­ian fairy tales and children’s sto­ries that I had pre­vi­ous­ly been exposed to. There were no child­ish hijinks, no young pro­tag­o­nists, no par­ents to res­cue you when you got into trou­ble. I con­sid­ered it an epic in the truest lit­er­ary sense.
As with many Russ­ian trans­la­tions dur­ing the Cold War, the book came with a com­plete­ly dif­fer­ent set of illus­tra­tions. Mine, I remem­ber regret­ting slight­ly, lacked pic­tures alto­geth­er. A friend’s edi­tion, how­ev­er, was illus­trat­ed in the typ­i­cal Russ­ian style: much more tra­di­tion­al­ly styl­ized than Tolkien’s own draw­ings, they were more angu­lar, friend­lier, almost car­toon­ish. In this post, we include a num­ber of these images from the 1976 print­ing. The cov­er, above, depicts a grin­ning Bil­bo Bag­gins hold­ing a gem. Below, Gan­dalf, an osten­si­bly harm­less soul, pays Bil­bo a vis­it.

Next, we have the three trolls, argu­ing about their var­i­ous eat­ing arrange­ments, with Bil­bo hid­ing to the side.

Here, Gol­lum, né Sméagol, pad­dles his raft in the depths of the moun­tains.

Final­ly, here’s Bil­bo, ful­fill­ing his role as a bur­glar in Smaug’s lair.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2014.
Ilia Blin­d­er­man is a Mon­tre­al-based cul­ture and sci­ence writer.

title: The Bialetti Moka Express: The History of Italy’s Iconic Coffee Maker, and How to Use It the Right Way
description:
in Food & Drink, History |   	October 13th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

I am sure that many an Open Cul­ture read­er has a Bialet­ti Moka Expres
body:
in Food & Drink, History |   	October 13th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

I am sure that many an Open Cul­ture read­er has a Bialet­ti Moka Express in their kitchen. I know I do, but I must add that I knew lit­tle about its his­to­ry and appar­ent­ly even less about how to prop­er­ly use one. Cof­fee expert and author of The World Atlas of Cof­fee James Hoff­mann intro­duces us to the appli­ance we think we know in the above video.
Alfon­so Bialet­ti didn’t orig­i­nal­ly get into the cof­fee busi­ness. In 1919, the Bialet­ti com­pa­ny was an alu­minum man­u­fac­tur­er, with the Moka Express invent­ed some­where around 1933 by Lui­gi de Pon­ti, who worked for the com­pa­ny. Accord­ing to Decon­struct­ing Prod­uct Design by William Lid­well and Ger­ry Man­ac­sa, the inspi­ra­tion came from Bialetti’s wife’s old-fash­ioned wash­ing machine: “a fire, a buck­et, and a lid with a tube com­ing out of it. The buck­et was filled with soapy water, sealed with the lid, and then brought to a boil over the fire, at which point the vapor­ized soapy water was pushed up through the tube and expelled on to the laun­dry.”
As Hoff­mann shows, ear­li­er cof­fee-mak­ers did use steam and a drip tech­nique, but the Moka Express was the first all-in-one mak­er that could sit on the stove top and do the work. All the user had to lis­ten for was the tell-tale gur­gle when it fin­ished brew­ing.


	

In 1945, Alfonso’s son Rena­to returned from a pris­on­er-of-war camp and took over the fam­i­ly busi­ness. He was instru­men­tal in focus­ing on the Moka Express and turn­ing it into an inter­na­tion­al cof­fee brand. He hired car­toon­ist Paul Cam­pani to design l’omino coi baf­fi, “the mus­ta­chioed lit­tle man” whose image is on the side of every Moka Express, and who, dur­ing the 1950s, was in a series of humor­ous ani­mat­ed com­mer­cials. Bialet­ti was the pride of Italy, and for Ital­ian immi­grants liv­ing abroad, it was a trea­sured object in the kitchen.
Such was the iden­ti­fi­ca­tion of Rena­to Bialet­ti with the Moka Express that when he died in 2016, his ash­es were interred in a giant repli­ca pot. Hoff­mann details the fate of the com­pa­ny after­wards, how it has fared against com­peti­tors in Italy and out­side. Will it still be around in decades? Who knows. But it does make a great cup of cof­fee.


	

And he shows the cor­rect way to brew a cup with the Moka Express in this oth­er video. Here are a few things I was doing wrong: not using hot water in the bot­tom to start; try­ing to pack in the ground cof­fee like I was mak­ing an espres­so; using too fine a grind; and not cool­ing the bot­tom as soon as it’s done work­ing its mag­ic. (Note: a Moka Express cof­fee is some­where between an espres­so and a pour-over.) All these tips I’m going to try tomor­row morn­ing. Maybe you have been mak­ing your Bialet­ti cup the right way all along. Let me know in the com­ments. I’ll read them over a fresh­ly brewed cup.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2022.

title: The Names of Nearly 4 Million Enslaved People in Former British Colonies Are Now Searchable Online, Helping Descendants Find Lost Ancestors
description:
in History |   	October 13th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
A few years ago, we fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture the Freedmen’s Bureau Project data­bas
body:
in History |   	October 13th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
A few years ago, we fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture the Freedmen’s Bureau Project data­base, which con­tains search­able infor­ma­tion on for­mer­ly enslaved peo­ple in the Unit­ed States after its Civ­il War. With near­ly 1.8 mil­lion men, women, and chil­dren reg­is­tered there when it first opened to the pub­lic, it has remained a valu­able resource for many Amer­i­cans research­ing their own her­itage, not just descen­dants of for­mer slaves but of oth­er Civ­il War refugees as well. But of course, the U.S. was hard­ly the only coun­try where slav­ery exist­ed. Count­less peo­ple here in the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry have ances­tors who were enslaved in oth­er for­mer British colonies, and now they’ve got a por­tal through which to do genealog­i­cal search­es of their own.
Launched by a part­ner­ship between the geneal­o­gy com­pa­ny Ances­try and the Cen­tre for the Study of the Lega­cies of British Slav­ery at Uni­ver­si­ty Col­lege Lon­don, the online For­mer British Colonies Enslave­ment Reg­is­ters makes avail­able records on near­ly four mil­lion indi­vid­u­als enslaved between 1813 and 1840 in a host of coun­tries from the Bahamas to Mau­ri­tius to South Africa.
First cre­at­ed by the British gov­ern­ment dur­ing the process of abol­ish­ing the transat­lantic slave trade in 1807 — much as the Freedmen’s Bureau orga­nized its reg­istry of for­mer slaves dur­ing Recon­struc­tion under Abra­ham Lin­coln — the orig­i­nal papers con­tain not just their names and ages, but also mater­nal fam­i­ly con­nec­tions, phys­i­cal descrip­tions, and some­times details about their place of African ori­gin.


	

In the video above, geneal­o­gist and Ances­try Senior Sto­ry Pro­duc­er Nic­ka Sewell-Smith pro­vides an intro­duc­tion to the For­mer British Colonies Enslave­ment Reg­is­ters, which you can access here. If you’re curi­ous about whether your own ances­tors may appear in its records, you can search by details like name, approx­i­mate date, or loca­tion to nar­row down the poten­tial match­es. The mod­ern descen­dants of peo­ple enslaved in the 20 coun­tries cov­ered by the data­base by no means live exclu­sive­ly, or even pri­mar­i­ly, in those coun­tries or in Great Britain itself. More than two cen­turies lat­er, their descen­dants live all over the world, includ­ing in Latin Amer­i­ca and the Unit­ed States, lead­ing lives very dif­fer­ent from those of their enslaved ances­tors — but the recon­struc­tion of their fam­i­ly sto­ries has only just begun. Enter the data­base here.
via Kot­tke
Relat­ed con­tent:
The Atlantic Slave Trade Visu­al­ized in Two Min­utes: 10 Mil­lion Lives, 20,000 Voy­ages, Over 315 Years
The Names of 1.8 Mil­lion Eman­ci­pat­ed Slaves Are Now Search­able in the World’s Largest Genealog­i­cal Data­base, Help­ing African Amer­i­cans Find Lost Ances­tors
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Meet the Lap Easel, a Portable Companion for Taking Creativity Anywhere
description: From birch plywood and select solid maple, birch, cherry, and other native hardwoods, Chicago maker and designer Bill Groot crafts handmade Lap Ea
body:
From birch plywood and select solid maple, birch, cherry, and other native hardwoods, Chicago maker and designer Bill Groot crafts handmade Lap Easels in small batches. The ingenious device is a portable, adjustable support that sits comfortably on your lap or tabletop. It’s perfect for a multitude of creative activities, like drawing and painting, reading books and magazines, writing, relaxing with a screen, holding a cookbook, and more.
The Lap Easel’s strong and lightweight design features five angled height settings to reduce hand and neck fatigue, and basic supplies can be tucked into the body compartment. Order yours today in the Colossal Shop.

title: 221 Camera Obscuras Fill Pneuhaus' Immersive, Inflatable, Image-Capturing Installation
description: At first glance, the structure resembles a kind of elongated igloo or a giant, white snail. One one hand, it’s an immersive, pop-up room with a fu
body:
At first glance, the structure resembles a kind of elongated igloo or a giant, white snail. One one hand, it’s an immersive, pop-up room with a futuristic, bubble-like texture. It’s also a giant, walk-in camera (there are 221 lenses to be exact). 
Premiering late last month at MODE Festival, a celebration of global photography, “Compound Camera 3” is the latest work by Pneuhaus, the Rhode Island-based studio known for its large-scale, architectural inflatables. Dozens of tiny cameras comprise the installation, which covers more than 700 square feet and invites visitors to walk around inside of a projection powered entirely by the sun. The images visible through the tiny apertures land on bulbous surfaces, and visitors can push on the soft material inside to distort what Pneuhaus describes as a “bug’s-eye view” of the sky and urban surroundings.

In our era of information, it’s impossible to describe Pneuhaus’ multi-lensed work without thinking about recent, crucial conversations about surveillance, especially when it comes to license plate readers and doorbell cameras that are tethered to enormous private data networks. In this case, though, the “information” is about being present. Nothing is recorded.
In “Compound Camera 3,” visitors step inside of a luminous viewing room, but there are no LED screens here; the sunlight simply illuminates everyday scenes through an essential analog method. Lenses pointing upward portray the sky across dozens of interior facets not unlike the structure of an insect’s eye. Those directed sideways show trees, buildings, and other people walking around. Everything appears multiplied, encouraging us to slow down and examine details more closely than we might if we were seeing the same scene just outside.
See more on Pneuhaus’ Instagram.

Photo by Lachlan Turczan


Photo by Stefan Stefanizyn

title: 'Arcana Borealis' Summons the Power of Spirituality and Artist Communities
description: Around 1906, Hilma af Klint was living in Stockholm, where she kept a studio. Deeply engaged with Christian esotericism, she channeled her mystic
body:
Around 1906, Hilma af Klint was living in Stockholm, where she kept a studio. Deeply engaged with Christian esotericism, she channeled her mystic visions into a series of otherworldly paintings that art historians acknowledge to be the first known abstract works in the canon, a paradigm shift in 20th-century art that had previously been credited to Wassily Kandinsky starting around 1910. 
What continues to awe us today about af Klint’s works is she didn’t view her vibrant paintings strictly as artworks, but as a result of spiritual channeling. Their production also coincided with a period of incredible scientific discovery. Nikola Tesla had just developed the alternating current (AC) electricity system, plus generated the first radio transmissions, when he then used to create a remote control. And 1905 was Einstein’s “miracle year” with the publication of his seminal theory of relativity.
Elga Sesemann, “Bird” (1968). Photo by Jenni Nurminen, courtesy of the Finnish National Gallery Collection/Ateneum Art Museum, Yrjö and Nanny Kaunisto Collection
A major exhibition titled Arcana Borealis—Northern Women and Esotericism deep-dives into the history of modern art through the lens of women artists working at the intersection of spirituality and esotericism. Opening soon at the Atenium Art Museum, part of the Finnish National Gallery, the show also explores the nature of artistic networks. In all, the exhibition gathers more than 200 works by 50 artists to broaden perspectives on women’s creative practices guided by belief systems, ecology, and the imagination.
Arcana Borealis features notable pieces by early 20th-century artists like af Klint and Anna Cassel alongside Anna-Eva Bergman, Maja Fjaestad, Sonja Ferlov Mancoba, and contemporary artist Outi Pieski. Visitors will encounter paintings, sculpture, textiles, stained glass, video, and much more that curators Dr. Nina Kokkinen and Dr. Marja Lahelma conceive as a challenge to “art historical narratives that have privileged the myth of the lone artistic genius,” the museum says. Instead, Arcana Borealis highlights how collaboration and spiritual communities shape the artists’ practices.
Cassel and af Klint worked together, for example, as part of what became known as The Five, a group of Stockholm-based women who explored spiritual realms through séances and meditation. Collaboration also comes to the fore in Pieski’s performance titled “Guhte gullá / Here to Hear.”
Pieski collaborated with dancers and choreographers Biret and Gáddjá Haarla Pieski, drawing on their Sámi heritage and incorporating vibrant clothing in a nod to traditional garments. The Sámi are an Indigenous people in predominantly the northern regions of Norway, Sweden, and Finland, and performance speaks to the trauma inflicted by state-sponsored assimilation programs and discrimination going back centuries.
Biret and Gáddjá Haarla Pieski, Outi Pieski, “Guhte gullá / Here to Hear” (2021). Photo by Mauri Lähdesmäki
The exhibition takes its title from the Latin arcana, meaning “hidden knowledge,” and borealis, meaning “the north.” The show “approaches ‘the North’ as a cross-border cultural and imaginative space shaped by mythology and spiritual traditions,” the museum says. “It traces how artists across Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Iceland, and Sápmi turned to esotericism, alternative cosmologies, meditation and mediumistic practices to explore questions of existence, creativity, and belonging.”
Arcana Borealis opens on October 23 and continues through February 28, 2027, in Helsinki. You might also enjoy navigating into the arcane through Taschen’s Tarot, part of the publisher’s Library of Esoterica series.
Anna Cassel, “Untitled II, No. 32” (1915), oil and metallic paint on canvas. Photo courtesy of The Hilma af Klint Foundation/Anders Fredriksén
Outi Pieski, “Beavvit (Rising Together)” (2019), knotted fringes in polyester thread, metal. Photo by Annar Brøgli, courtesy of the National Museum for Art, Architecture and Design, Oslo
Laila Pullinen, “Mata Hari IV” (1965). Photo by Aleks Talve, courtesy of the Finnish National Gallery Collection/Ateneum Art Museum
Anna Cassel, “Untitled II, No. 62” (1915), oil on canvas. Photo courtesy of The Hilma af Klint Foundation/Anders Fredriksén
Rita Kernn-Larsen, “Oasis” (1935), oil on canvas, 109 x 79 centimeters. © Rita Kernn-Larsen / VISDA, courtesy of Randers Art Museum
Tyra Kleen, “Forbidden Fruit” (1909), gouache on paper. Photo © Bobo Lindblad, Lindblad Studio, courtesy of Riddarhuset, Tyra Kleen Collection
Sonja Ferlov Mancoba, “Mask and Figure” (1984), bronze. Photo by Lars Bay, courtesy of Randers Art Museum
Anna Cassel, “Untitled II, No. 33” (1915), oil and metallic paint on canvas. Photo courtesy of The Hilma af Klint Foundation/Anders Fredriksén

title: Karachi Biennale Cancels Fifth Edition Over “War Conditions”
description:
News
                The cancellation of the January 2027 event reportedly came without the input of the biennale’s curator, Noo
body:
News
                The cancellation of the January 2027 event reportedly came without the input of the biennale’s curator, Noor Ahmed.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Adeela Suleman’s outdoor installation, "The Killing Fields of Karachi," at the 2019 Karachi Biennale (photo courtesy Adeela Suleman)
    
        
            The Karachi Biennale in Pakistan announced the cancellation of its fifth edition in an Instagram statement on Friday, October 9, citing logistical constraints and uncertainties amid "war conditions prevailing in the region."Originally scheduled for January 16 through January 31, the biennale was to welcome artists to Karachi, the largest city in Pakistan and the capital of its Sindh province. It is not yet clear what specific circumstances or events in the region contributed to the cancellation, which reportedly occurred without the input of the biennale’s curator, Noor Ahmed, according to the Pakistani newspaper Dawn’s cultural imprint, Images."Artists and partners have been contacting me and they are all quite disappointed about how communications and commitments with them are being handled," Ahmed told Hyperallergic. For the past 13 months, she engaged over 100 artists and practices for the biennale and enlisted three individuals to co-curate sections of the event.  The Karachi Biennale Trust, which organizes the event, has not replied to Hyperallergic's immediate request for comment.
